name: APGAR score
seoDesc: APGAR score: work out respiration from the APGAR score. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The APGAR score calculator returns respiration from the 5 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the APGAR score calculator work?
sections.html:
The APGAR score calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports respiration in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the skin color (Appearance), the heart rate (Pulse) and the reflex irritability (Grimace)); then you type in the APGAR score.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as blue or pale all over, blue at extremities, body pink and pink all over. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as absent, < 100 beats per minute and > 100 beats per minute. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as no response to stimulation, grimace on stimulation and cry or active withdrawal on stimulation. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as none, muscles are limp, some flexion and active motion, flexed arms and legs. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A number, expressed in pts.

5 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the APGAR score calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Respiration=-muscle tone (Activity) + APGAR score − skin color (Appearance) − reflex irritability (Grimace) − heart rate (Pulse)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The APGAR score calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the APGAR score — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the APGAR score calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns respiration, derived from the APGAR score. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the APGAR score calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the APGAR score, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports APGAR score = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the APGAR score calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
